description: Comprehensive question bank derived from 'Movements of Earth' PDF. Covers rotation, revolution, Coriolis effect, seasons, solstices, equinoxes, perihelion/aphelion, axial tilt, leap year, day/night length, polar day/night, and common exam traps. No duplicate questions; every key point from the source is represented.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are the two principal movements of Earth?

options.B: Precession and nutation

questions.explanation: The two principal movements of Earth are rotation on its axis and revolution in its orbit around the Sun.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is rotation of Earth?

options.A: The orbital movement around the Sun
options.B: The spinning movement around its imaginary axis
options.C: The slow change in axis direction
options.D: The elliptical path around the Sun

questions.explanation: Rotation is the spinning movement of Earth around its imaginary axis, which passes through the North Pole and South Pole.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is revolution of Earth?

options.A: The spinning movement on its axis
options.B: The orbital movement around the Sun along a slightly elliptical path
options.D: The daily cycle of day and night

questions.explanation: Revolution is the orbital movement of Earth around the Sun along a slightly elliptical path.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the main difference between rotation and revolution?

options.A: Rotation causes seasons; revolution causes day and night
options.B: Rotation is spinning on its axis and produces day/night; revolution is orbital movement around the Sun and with axial tilt produces seasons
options.C: Rotation is orbital movement; revolution is spinning on its axis
options.E: Rotation causes seasons; revolution causes precession

questions.explanation: Rotation is Earth's spinning on its own axis and produces the daily cycle of day and night; revolution is Earth's orbital movement around the Sun and, together with axial tilt, produces the annual cycle of seasons.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is Earth's axis?

options.A: An imaginary line passing through the geographic North Pole and South Pole
options.B: The plane of Earth's orbit
options.C: The apparent path of the Sun
options.D: The line connecting Earth and the Sun

questions.explanation: Earth's axis is an imaginary line passing through the geographic North Pole and South Pole, around which Earth rotates.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Is Earth's axis fixed in space?

options.B: It maintains an approximately constant direction over one year but slowly changes orientation over long periods due to precession and other motions
options.C: No, it changes direction every day
options.E: It is fixed relative to the Sun

questions.explanation: Earth's axis maintains an approximately constant direction over the course of one year, but it slowly changes orientation over long periods due to precession and other motions.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the orbital plane of Earth?

options.B: The imaginary flat plane containing Earth's path around the Sun
options.D: The plane of the celestial equator
options.E: The plane passing through the poles

questions.explanation: The orbital plane is the imaginary flat plane containing Earth's path around the Sun; it is also called the plane of the ecliptic.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the ecliptic?

options.A: The apparent annual path of the Sun against the background stars
options.B: The path of the Moon around Earth
options.E: The path of Earth around the Moon

questions.explanation: The ecliptic is the apparent annual path of the Sun against the background stars as viewed from Earth and corresponds to the plane of Earth's orbit projected onto the celestial sphere.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: In which direction does Earth rotate?

options.B: West to east
options.E: Clockwise when viewed from above the North Pole

questions.explanation: Earth rotates from west to east, which is counterclockwise when viewed from above the North Pole.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How long does Earth take to complete one rotation relative to distant stars?

options.B: 23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds

questions.explanation: Earth takes approximately 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4 seconds to complete one rotation relative to distant stars; this is called a sidereal day.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How long is a mean solar day on Earth?

options.B: Approximately 23 hours 56 minutes

questions.explanation: A mean solar day is approximately 24 hours, which is the average time between successive passages of the mean Sun across a local meridian.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why is a solar day longer than a sidereal day?

options.A: Because Earth rotates faster than it revolves
options.B: Because while rotating, Earth also moves forward in its orbit, so it must rotate slightly more than 360° for the Sun to return to the same meridian
options.C: Because the Moon slows Earth's rotation
options.D: Because the Sun moves around Earth

questions.explanation: While Earth rotates on its axis, it also moves forward along its orbit around the Sun; it must rotate slightly more than 360° for the Sun to return to the same apparent meridian position.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the angular speed of Earth's rotation?

options.B: About 1° per hour

questions.explanation: Earth rotates through approximately 360° in 24 hours, giving an average angular speed of about 15° per hour or 15 arcminutes per minute.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the linear rotational speed at the Equator?

options.B: Approximately 1,000 km/h

questions.explanation: The linear rotational speed at the Equator is approximately 1,670 kilometres per hour, or about 465 metres per second.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does the linear speed of rotation change from the Equator towards the poles?

options.B: It decreases with increasing latitude and becomes zero at the geographic poles
options.C: It remains constant at all latitudes
options.D: It becomes maximum at the poles

questions.explanation: The linear speed of Earth's surface due to rotation decreases with increasing latitude and becomes zero at the geographic poles, although angular rotation rate is the same at all latitudes.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why is rotational linear speed greatest at the Equator?

options.B: Because the Equator has the largest circular path around Earth's axis, so a point there travels the greatest distance in the same rotation period
options.C: Because the Equator is closest to the Moon
options.D: Because the angular speed is highest there
options.E: Because the Equator is tilted towards the Sun

questions.explanation: The Equator has the largest circular path around Earth's axis, so a point there travels the greatest distance in the same rotation period.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the rotational speed at the geographic poles?

options.B: Zero

questions.explanation: The linear speed due to rotation is effectively zero at the exact poles because the poles lie on the axis of rotation.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the direction of Earth's rotation when viewed from above the South Pole?

options.B: Clockwise

questions.explanation: Earth appears to rotate clockwise when viewed from above the South Pole.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the difference between angular speed and linear speed of Earth's rotation?

options.A: Angular speed is the same for all points; linear speed is greatest at the Equator and zero at the poles
options.B: Angular speed is greatest at the Equator; linear speed is the same everywhere
options.D: Angular speed varies with latitude; linear speed is constant
options.E: Angular speed is zero at the poles; linear speed is maximum there

questions.explanation: Angular speed measures the angle turned per unit time and is essentially the same for all points on Earth; linear speed measures distance travelled per unit time and is greatest at the Equator and zero at the poles.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the most important effect of Earth's rotation?

options.B: The regular alternation of day and night

questions.explanation: The most familiar effect of Earth's rotation is the regular alternation of day and night.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does Earth's rotation cause day and night?

options.B: The half of Earth facing the Sun experiences daylight, while the half turned away experiences night; rotation carries places alternately into and out of sunlight
options.C: Earth's orbit brings it closer to and farther from the Sun
options.D: Axial tilt causes day and night

questions.explanation: At any moment, the half of Earth facing the Sun experiences daylight, while the half turned away from the Sun experiences night; rotation carries places alternately into and out of sunlight.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why does the Sun appear to rise in the east and set in the west?

options.A: Because the Sun moves east to west
options.B: Because Earth rotates from west to east, making the Sun and other celestial objects appear to move from east to west
options.C: Because Earth revolves around the Sun

questions.explanation: Earth rotates from west to east, making the Sun and other celestial objects appear to move across the sky from east to west.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does Earth's rotation affect the apparent daily movement of stars?

options.A: Stars appear to move from east to west, completing an apparent daily circuit around the celestial poles
options.B: Stars appear to move from west to east
options.E: Stars move only during the day

questions.explanation: Earth's rotation makes stars appear to move from east to west across the sky, completing an apparent daily circuit around the celestial poles.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does Earth's rotation contribute to the difference in local time between longitudes?

options.A: Local solar time changes by approximately one hour for every 15° of longitude, or four minutes for every one degree
options.B: Local time changes by one hour per 30° of longitude
options.C: Local time is the same at all longitudes
options.D: Local time changes by two hours per 15°
options.E: Local time changes by four minutes per 15°

questions.explanation: As Earth rotates 360° in about 24 hours, local solar time changes by approximately one hour for every 15° of longitude, or four minutes for every one degree.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does Earth's rotation contribute to the development of time zones?

options.A: Differences in local solar time led to standard time zones, generally based on bands of longitude, with political adjustments
options.B: Time zones are based on latitude
options.C: Time zones are based on the Moon's position
options.D: Time zones are based on axial tilt
options.E: Time zones are based on revolution

questions.explanation: Differences in local solar time caused by Earth's rotation led to the adoption of standard time zones, generally based on bands of longitude, with political adjustments.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does Earth's rotation affect the shape of Earth?

options.A: It makes Earth a perfect sphere
options.B: It contributes to the equatorial bulge and polar flattening, making Earth an oblate spheroid
options.C: It makes Earth a prolate spheroid
options.D: It has no effect on shape
options.E: It makes Earth perfectly flat at the equator

questions.explanation: Rotation contributes to the equatorial bulge and polar flattening, making Earth an oblate spheroid rather than a perfect sphere.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does Earth's rotation influence ocean currents and winds?

options.A: It produces the Coriolis effect, which deflects large-scale moving air and water and helps shape global wind and ocean-current patterns
options.B: It has no effect on ocean currents

questions.explanation: Earth's rotation produces the Coriolis effect, which deflects large-scale moving air and water relative to Earth's surface and helps shape global wind and ocean-current patterns.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does Earth's rotation cause the seasons?

options.B: No, axial tilt combined with revolution causes seasons
options.D: Yes, but only in the Northern Hemisphere

questions.explanation: No. Earth's axial tilt combined with its revolution around the Sun causes the seasons; rotation causes the daily cycle of day and night.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does Earth's rotation cause the annual change in the Sun's overhead position?

options.B: No, the annual north-south shift is caused by Earth's axial tilt as Earth revolves around the Sun
options.D: Yes, but only at the Equator
options.E: No, it is caused by perihelion

questions.explanation: No. The annual north-south shift in the Sun's apparent overhead position is caused by Earth's axial tilt as Earth revolves around the Sun.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the Coriolis effect?

options.A: The apparent deflection of moving objects when their motion is observed in a rotating reference frame such as Earth
options.B: The bending of light in the atmosphere
options.C: The change in Earth's rotation speed
options.D: The gravitational pull of the Moon

questions.explanation: The Coriolis effect is the apparent deflection of moving objects, including air and water, when their motion is observed in a rotating reference frame such as Earth.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why is the Coriolis effect produced on Earth?

options.A: Because Earth rotates and different latitudes have different eastward linear velocities
options.B: Because Earth revolves around the Sun

questions.explanation: It arises because Earth rotates and different latitudes have different eastward linear velocities; moving air and water retain momentum as they move across latitudes.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Who is the Coriolis effect named after?

options.B: Isaac Newton

questions.explanation: It is named after the French mathematician and engineer Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, who described the effect mathematically in 1835.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: In which direction are moving objects deflected in the Northern Hemisphere by the Coriolis effect?

options.A: To the right of their direction of motion
options.B: To the left of their direction of motion

questions.explanation: They are deflected to the right of their direction of motion in the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: In which direction are moving objects deflected in the Southern Hemisphere by the Coriolis effect?

options.B: To the left

questions.explanation: They are deflected to the left of their direction of motion in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: At which latitude is the horizontal Coriolis effect zero?

options.B: At the Tropic of Cancer

questions.explanation: The horizontal Coriolis effect is zero at the Equator.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Where is the Coriolis effect strongest for horizontal motion?

options.B: At the Equator

questions.explanation: For horizontal motion, the Coriolis effect is strongest at the poles and zero at the Equator.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does the Coriolis effect influence winds?

options.A: It deflects large-scale moving air, helping shape prevailing winds, global atmospheric circulation and the rotation of weather systems
options.B: It has no effect on winds
options.C: It causes winds to blow straight from pole to equator

questions.explanation: It deflects large-scale moving air, helping shape prevailing winds, global atmospheric circulation and the rotation of weather systems.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does the Coriolis effect influence ocean currents?

options.A: It deflects large-scale ocean currents and helps determine their directions and circulation patterns
options.B: It has no effect on ocean currents

questions.explanation: It deflects large-scale ocean currents and helps determine their directions and circulation patterns, together with winds, pressure gradients, coastlines and other factors.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How do large low-pressure cyclones rotate in the Northern Hemisphere?

options.B: Clockwise

questions.explanation: Large low-pressure cyclones generally rotate counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere because of the pressure-gradient force combined with the Coriolis effect and friction.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How do large low-pressure cyclones rotate in the Southern Hemisphere?

options.B: Clockwise

questions.explanation: Large low-pressure cyclones generally rotate clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why do tropical cyclones rarely form very close to the Equator?

options.A: The Coriolis effect is too weak near the Equator to provide the necessary initial rotation
options.B: The temperature is too high

questions.explanation: The Coriolis effect is too weak near the Equator to provide the necessary initial rotation for typical tropical cyclone development.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does the Coriolis effect determine the direction water drains from an ordinary household sink?

options.A: Yes, always counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere
options.B: Yes, always clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere
options.C: No, at household scale basin shape, water motion, plumbing and other local conditions dominate; the Coriolis effect is far too weak to reliably determine the direction
options.D: Yes, but only in the Southern Hemisphere
options.E: Yes, but only at the Equator

questions.explanation: At household scale, basin shape, water motion, plumbing and other local conditions dominate; the Coriolis effect is far too weak to reliably determine the direction.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Is the Coriolis force a real force in an inertial reference frame?

options.A: Yes, it is a fundamental force
options.B: No, it is a fictitious or apparent force introduced when motion is described from a rotating reference frame
options.C: Yes, it is a gravitational force
options.D: Yes, it is an electromagnetic force
options.E: No, it does not exist at all

questions.explanation: The Coriolis force is a fictitious or apparent force introduced when motion is described from a rotating reference frame; it is useful in equations for motion relative to Earth.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the formula for the magnitude of the horizontal Coriolis parameter?

options.B: f = Ω cos φ

questions.explanation: The Coriolis parameter is f = 2Ω sin φ, where Ω is Earth's angular rotation rate and φ is latitude; it is zero at the Equator and has maximum magnitude at the poles.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the shape of Earth's orbit around the Sun?

options.B: A slightly elliptical orbit with the Sun at one focus

questions.explanation: Earth follows a slightly elliptical orbit around the Sun, with the Sun located at one focus of the ellipse.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: In which direction does Earth revolve around the Sun when viewed from above the North Pole?

options.B: Counterclockwise

questions.explanation: Earth revolves around the Sun in a counterclockwise direction when viewed from above the North Pole.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How long does Earth take to complete one sidereal revolution around the Sun?

options.B: 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes and 10 seconds

questions.explanation: Earth takes approximately 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes and 10 seconds to complete one sidereal revolution around the Sun.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a tropical year?

options.A: The time between successive passages of the Sun across the Equator
options.B: The average interval between successive occurrences of the same seasonal reference point, such as the March equinox
options.C: The time for one sidereal revolution
options.D: The time between perihelion and aphelion

questions.explanation: A tropical year is the average interval between successive occurrences of the same seasonal reference point, such as the March equinox; it is approximately 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes and 45 seconds.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the average orbital speed of Earth around the Sun?

options.B: Approximately 1,670 km/h

questions.explanation: Earth's average orbital speed is approximately 29.8 kilometres per second, or about 107,000 kilometres per hour.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does Earth's orbital speed remain constant throughout the year?

options.B: No, it increases as Earth approaches the Sun and decreases as it moves farther away
options.E: No, it is faster in July

questions.explanation: Earth's orbital speed increases as it approaches the Sun and decreases as it moves farther away, in accordance with Kepler's second law.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun called?

options.B: The equatorial plane

questions.explanation: The plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun is called the ecliptic plane.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the main geographical significance of Earth's revolution?

options.B: Together with the tilt of its axis, it causes the annual cycle of seasons and changes in the length of daylight at different latitudes

questions.explanation: Earth's revolution, together with the tilt of its axis, causes the annual cycle of seasons and changes in the length of daylight at different latitudes.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does Earth's revolution alone cause seasons?

options.B: No, seasons occur because Earth revolves around the Sun while its rotational axis is tilted and maintains nearly the same direction in space
options.C: Yes, along with distance from the Sun
options.D: Yes, but only in the Southern Hemisphere

questions.explanation: No. Seasons occur because Earth revolves around the Sun while its rotational axis is tilted and maintains nearly the same direction in space during the annual orbit.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are the major effects of Earth's revolution combined with axial tilt?

options.A: The annual cycle of seasons, changing apparent position of the overhead Sun between the tropics, variation in day and night length, solstices, equinoxes and polar day and polar night
options.B: Only the alternation of day and night

questions.explanation: The major effects include the annual cycle of seasons, the changing apparent position of the overhead Sun between the tropics, variation in day and night length, solstices, equinoxes and polar day and polar night.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why does the apparent position of the overhead Sun shift during the year?

options.A: Because Earth's axis is tilted, so the Sun's direct rays shift northward and southward between the Tropics
options.B: Because Earth's orbit is circular
options.D: Because the Sun moves around Earth

questions.explanation: Because Earth's axis is tilted, the Sun's direct rays shift northward and southward between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn during the annual revolution.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the apparent annual movement of the Sun?

options.A: The apparent north-south movement between approximately 23½° N and 23½° S latitude during the year
options.B: The apparent east-west movement between longitudes
options.C: The apparent daily movement across the sky
options.D: The apparent movement around the celestial poles
options.E: The apparent movement from perihelion to aphelion

questions.explanation: It is the apparent north-south movement of the Sun's overhead position between approximately 23½° N and 23½° S latitude during the year.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the significance of the June solstice?

options.A: Around 20 or 21 June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted most directly towards the Sun, the Sun is overhead near the Tropic of Cancer, and the Northern Hemisphere has its longest daylight period
options.B: Around 21 or 22 December, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun
options.C: The Sun is directly overhead at the Equator
options.D: Day and night are equal everywhere
options.E: Earth is closest to the Sun

questions.explanation: Around 20 or 21 June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted most directly towards the Sun, the Sun is overhead near the Tropic of Cancer, and the Northern Hemisphere has its longest daylight period of the year.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the significance of the December solstice?

options.A: Around 20 or 21 June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun
options.B: Around 21 or 22 December, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted most directly towards the Sun, the Sun is overhead near the Tropic of Capricorn, and the Northern Hemisphere has its shortest daylight period
options.C: The Sun is directly overhead at the Equator
options.D: Day and night are equal everywhere
options.E: Earth is farthest from the Sun

questions.explanation: Around 21 or 22 December, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted most directly towards the Sun, the Sun is overhead near the Tropic of Capricorn, and the Northern Hemisphere has its shortest daylight period of the year.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the significance of the equinoxes?

options.A: The Sun is directly overhead at the Equator and day and night are approximately equal in length across much of Earth
options.B: The Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer
options.C: The Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn
options.D: Earth is closest to the Sun
options.E: Earth is farthest from the Sun

questions.explanation: At the equinoxes, the Sun is directly overhead at the Equator and day and night are approximately equal in length across much of Earth.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why are the seasons opposite in the two hemispheres?

options.A: Because Earth's distance from the Sun changes
options.B: When one hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun and receives more direct sunlight and longer days, the other is tilted away and receives less direct sunlight and shorter days
options.C: Because the Sun moves around Earth
options.E: Because Earth rotates in opposite directions in the two hemispheres

questions.explanation: When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun and receives more direct sunlight and longer days, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted away and receives less direct sunlight and shorter days, and vice versa.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does Earth become significantly closer to the Sun during summer in the Northern Hemisphere?

options.B: No, Northern Hemisphere summer occurs near aphelion, when Earth is farthest from the Sun; axial tilt is the main cause of seasons
options.D: No, Earth is closest during Northern Hemisphere summer
options.E: Yes, this is why summers are hot

questions.explanation: No. Northern Hemisphere summer occurs near aphelion, when Earth is farthest from the Sun; axial tilt, not Earth-Sun distance, is the main cause of seasons.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What causes the seasons on Earth?

options.B: Earth's axial tilt of about 23.4° together with Earth's revolution around the Sun

questions.explanation: The seasons are caused primarily by Earth's axial tilt of about 23.4° relative to the perpendicular to its orbital plane, together with Earth's revolution around the Sun.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the angle of Earth's axial tilt?

options.A: Approximately 23.4° from the perpendicular to the orbital plane
options.B: Approximately 66.6° from the perpendicular to the orbital plane

questions.explanation: Earth's axis is tilted approximately 23.4° from the perpendicular to the plane of its orbit, equivalent to about 66.6° from the orbital plane itself.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the difference between axial tilt measured from the perpendicular and from the orbital plane?

options.A: The tilt is about 23.4° from the perpendicular and about 66.6° from the plane of the orbit; these are complementary angles
options.B: Both are 23.4°
options.E: The tilt is 90° from the perpendicular

questions.explanation: The tilt is about 23.4° from the perpendicular to the orbital plane and about 66.6° from the plane of the orbit; these are complementary angles.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why does a hemisphere experience summer when it is tilted towards the Sun?

options.A: It receives more direct solar rays and generally has longer daylight hours, increasing the amount of solar energy received per day
options.B: It is closer to the Sun

questions.explanation: It receives more direct solar rays and generally has longer daylight hours, increasing the amount of solar energy received per day.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why does a hemisphere experience winter when it is tilted away from the Sun?

options.A: It is farther from the Sun
options.B: It receives less direct solar rays and generally has shorter daylight hours, reducing the amount of solar energy received per day

questions.explanation: It receives less direct solar rays and generally has shorter daylight hours, reducing the amount of solar energy received per day.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are the four astronomical seasons in the Northern Hemisphere?

options.B: Wet, dry, hot and cold

questions.explanation: The four astronomical seasons are spring, summer, autumn (fall) and winter.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are the four astronomical seasons in the Southern Hemisphere?

options.A: Spring, summer, autumn and winter, but they occur at opposite times of the year compared with the Northern Hemisphere
options.B: Only wet and dry seasons
options.C: The same seasons at the same times as the Northern Hemisphere

questions.explanation: The four astronomical seasons are also spring, summer, autumn and winter, but they occur at opposite times of the year compared with the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: When does spring begin astronomically in the Northern Hemisphere?

options.A: At the March or vernal equinox, usually around 20 March
options.B: At the June solstice, usually around 21 June
options.C: At the September equinox, usually around 22 September
options.D: At the December solstice, usually around 21 December

questions.explanation: Northern Hemisphere spring begins at the March or vernal equinox, usually around 20 March.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: When does summer begin astronomically in the Northern Hemisphere?

options.B: At the June or summer solstice, usually around 20 or 21 June

questions.explanation: Northern Hemisphere summer begins at the June or summer solstice, usually around 20 or 21 June.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: When does autumn begin astronomically in the Northern Hemisphere?

options.B: At the June solstice
options.C: At the September or autumnal equinox, usually around 22 or 23 September

questions.explanation: Northern Hemisphere autumn begins at the September or autumnal equinox, usually around 22 or 23 September.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: When does winter begin astronomically in the Northern Hemisphere?

options.B: At the June solstice
options.D: At the December or winter solstice, usually around 21 or 22 December

questions.explanation: Northern Hemisphere winter begins at the December or winter solstice, usually around 21 or 22 December.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: When does summer occur in the Southern Hemisphere?

options.A: Approximately from the December solstice to the March equinox
options.B: Approximately from the June solstice to the September equinox
options.C: Approximately from the March equinox to the June solstice
options.D: Approximately from the September equinox to the December solstice

questions.explanation: Southern Hemisphere summer occurs approximately from the December solstice to the March equinox.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: When does winter occur in the Southern Hemisphere?

options.A: Approximately from the December solstice to the March equinox
options.B: Approximately from the June solstice to the September equinox
options.C: Approximately from the March equinox to the June solstice
options.D: Approximately from the September equinox to the December solstice

questions.explanation: Southern Hemisphere winter occurs approximately from the June solstice to the September equinox.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Do all parts of Earth experience four sharply defined seasons?

options.B: No, the four-season model is most applicable to temperate regions; tropical regions often describe wet and dry seasons, while polar regions have extreme seasonal daylight changes
options.E: No, only the Northern Hemisphere has seasons

questions.explanation: No. The four-season model is most applicable to temperate regions; tropical regions often describe wet and dry seasons, while polar regions have extreme seasonal daylight changes.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a solstice?

options.A: One of the two annual moments when the Sun reaches its greatest apparent angular distance north or south of the celestial equator, producing the longest or shortest daylight period for a hemisphere
options.B: When the Sun crosses the celestial equator
options.C: When Earth is closest to the Sun
